opus-5.5.text:
I think of reinforcement learning from human feedback as a way of shaping the distribution a language model has already learned, rather than teaching it fundamentally new capabilities. When you pretrain a model on internet-scale text, it learns an enormous range of behaviors: helpful answers, unhelpful answers, toxic content, careful reasoning, sloppy reasoning, all mixed together. The model is essentially a very good density model over all of that. What RLHF does is say: out of all the things you could produce, these are the ones people actually prefer, so shift your probability mass toward them.

One way I like to view it, which connects to a lot of my own work on energy-based models and compositional generation, is that the reward model you learn from human preferences acts almost like an energy function, a score that tells you how compatible a given output is with what humans want. Fine-tuning the policy with RL, or with related methods like direct preference optimization, is then a way of sampling from the product of the original language model distribution and this preference-based distribution. You're composing two sources of knowledge: the broad world knowledge from pretraining and a narrower signal about human values and intentions.

That perspective also helps explain some of its limitations. The reward model is learned from a fairly limited set of comparisons, so it's only reliable near the data it was trained on. If you optimize too hard against it, the model finds outputs that score highly but aren't actually good, which is the classic reward hacking or overoptimization problem. That's why in practice you keep a KL penalty to stay close to the original model. You're trusting the preference signal only so far.

I also think RLHF is better at improving things like style, tone, helpfulness, and refusing clearly harmful requests than at instilling genuine reasoning or factual reliability. If the underlying model doesn't have a capability, preference tuning can't really conjure it. It can make the model sound more confident or more polished, which can sometimes even mask errors.

Going forward, I'm excited about ways to make that feedback richer and more structured: decomposing preferences into multiple components that can be composed, using verification and planning at inference time rather than baking everything into the weights, and getting feedback that's grounded in outcomes in the world rather than just which of two responses a person liked better. RLHF was a really important step for making these models usable, but I see it as one piece of a larger picture of how we align and steer generative models.

r001.rationale: The response explains that human preferences identify which outputs people prefer, and RLHF shifts probability mass toward those outputs.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about RLHF is that it's really a way of getting a model to be useful rather than just getting it to be good at predicting text. When you pretrain a language model, you're training it to model the distribution of everything on the internet, and that distribution contains a lot of things you don't actually want: it contains incorrect answers, it contains people being rude to each other, it contains text that trails off and never actually answers the question. So the pretrained model knows how to do a lot of things, but it doesn't really know which of those things you want it to do.

What RLHF gives you is a way to express that preference without having to write it down explicitly. It's very hard to specify in a loss function what a "helpful" or "honest" response looks like. But it's relatively easy for a person to look at two responses and say, "this one is better." So you collect a lot of those comparisons, you train a reward model that captures that judgment, and then you optimize the language model against that reward. In a sense, you're letting humans define the objective by example rather than by formula.

I think the thing that's interesting to me, coming from more of a generative modeling and decision-making background, is that this is really a shift in what the model is being asked to do. Pretraining is about imitation: match the data. RLHF is about optimization: produce outputs that score well under some evaluator. And once you frame it that way, a lot of the failure modes become pretty predictable. If your reward model is imperfect, and it always is, the policy will find ways to exploit it. You get responses that sound confident and polished because people rated those highly, even when the content isn't right. You get the model learning what graders like rather than learning what's actually true.

So I'd say RLHF is extremely effective at the behavioral layer. It takes a model that's capable but unfocused and makes it follow instructions, stay on topic, decline things it should decline, and generally be pleasant to interact with. Where I'm more skeptical is the idea that it fundamentally improves the model's underlying reasoning or knowledge. It's mostly reshaping how the existing capability gets expressed. And that's why I think a lot of the current excitement is around moving beyond pure human preference toward reward signals that are more grounded: did the code actually run, did the math check out, is the answer verifiable. Those kinds of rewards are harder to game, and I think they're where a lot of the real capability gains are going to come from.

r001.rationale: The response explains that people compare model responses, those judgments train a reward model, and the language model is optimized against that reward—making outputs judged better more likely.

astra-6.text:
I think of reinforcement learning with human feedback as a way of steering a language model toward responses that people find useful. During pretraining, the model learns to predict text, but predicting text well doesn’t necessarily mean answering a question in the way a person wants.

With human feedback, you can have people compare different responses and use those preferences to train a reward model. Then you optimize the language model to produce responses that score well under that reward model. That can make it better at following instructions and interacting with users.

The limitation is that human preference is a proxy for what we actually care about. A response might sound convincing without being correct, and people might reward that. So I see it as a useful tool for shaping behavior, but it doesn’t by itself guarantee factual accuracy or reliable reasoning.

r001.rationale: It explains that people compare responses to provide preferences, those preferences train a reward model, and the language model is optimized to produce responses that score well—making human-preferred outputs more likely.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of reinforcement learning with human feedback as a way of shaping a language model’s behavior after it has learned to predict text. Predicting what comes next on the internet isn’t quite the same thing as giving a useful answer to someone’s question. Human feedback provides a signal about which responses people actually prefer, and reinforcement learning can use that signal to make those responses more likely.

The limitation is that preference is an imperfect measure of correctness. An answer can sound convincing and receive positive feedback while still being wrong. So I think it’s a useful tool for improving how models interact with people, but it doesn’t, by itself, guarantee that they’re reliable or that they understand what they’re saying.

r001.rationale: The response says human feedback signals which outputs people prefer and that reinforcement learning uses this signal to make those responses more likely.
